reason: The text presents the opposite moral: when the Israelites cry out to God (וַיִּזְעֲקוּ בְנֵֽי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶל־ יְהוָֽה), their complaint is answered positively by God sending a deliverer. Even when Gideon questions God (לָ֥מָּה מְצָאַ֖תְנוּ כָּל־ זֹ֑את—'Why has all this befallen us?'), God does not rebuke him for complaining but instead empowers him for service. The narrative structure suggests that crying out in distress is the appropriate response to oppression, and it leads to divine intervention. The story's actual moral concerns faith, obedience to God's call, and trust in divine deliverance—not discouraging people from voicing their grievances.
